title: What the homepage has to prove for a logistics company
metaTitle: What a logistics homepage must prove
excerpt: Show a real move, not a globe or a stock container, then a way to request a quote. An operator with a dock and a cutoff will not infer the work from a map.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, for a homepage that should name the freight as plainly as a title you can read.
caption: Crates of used books with the titles facing out. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a logistics homepage show?
faqs.answer: Show one move an operator would recognize: places, the freight, and a fact about how it ran, such as an appointment kept or a POD returned. Then offer a way to request a quote, with the few facts the quote needs. A globe, a skyline, or a stock container does not answer whether you can move their freight.

faqs.question: What if we cannot publish a customer's shipment?
faqs.answer: Use a clearly labeled sample built from work you actually take, with realistic weight, equipment, and geography. Or describe the move in type without a photograph. Do not substitute a rented image of a container. Strip any detail a customer did not agree to show.

faqs.question: Where should tracking sit on the homepage?
faqs.answer: Tracking belongs in the header for someone who already has a reference number. It should not share equal weight with the quote on the first screen. The first screen is for the operator deciding whether you get the freight. People who already shipped with you know why they came.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The logistics company homepage has one job for an operator who needs to know you can move the thing. Show the work, then offer a way to request a quote. A globe does not do that. A stock photo of a shipping container does not do it either. Write the page in that order.

The operator is often a person with a dock, a cutoff, and a boss who will ask where the freight is. They are not browsing for a feeling about global trade. If the first screen cannot name a move, they will go to the carrier who can.

## Show a move, not a map

Put one shipment in the first screen. Origin and destination in the form an operator uses: city to city, or port to warehouse, not "coast to coast" as a mood. What it was: pallets, a machine, a temperature-controlled load, a last-mile delivery with a liftgate. What happened that they would recognize as competence: it made the appointment, it was reweighed and the quote held, the POD was back the same day.

If the move is real, use it, and strip anything the customer did not agree to publish. If you are using a sample, label it as a sample and keep the numbers realistic for the work you actually take. A cartoon container on a beach is not a sample. It is a different industry's postcard.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave a page in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and that the value has to be clear within about 10 seconds if you want a longer visit. For this homepage, value is the move. The operator should be able to say, before they scroll, what you carried and how to ask for a price.

Leave the rotating globe, the network diagram with unnamed dots, and the drone shot of an anonymous port for a sales deck if you must. They tell the team that the company is large. They tell the operator nothing about the next truck.

## Then the quote, in the same screen

The action is to request a quote, and the label should say that. "Request a quote" is plain and correct. "Let's connect" is a meeting. "Get started" is a software trial. The operator came to price a move.

Say, in one line under the button, what the quote needs. Origin, destination, ready date, weight or pallet count, and what is in the shipment. They already know these facts. Asking for them is not friction. Hiding them until a salesperson calls is friction, because the operator will assume you cannot price without a performance.

If you can return a number the same day for a standard lane, say so, and name the clock. "Quotes for standard LTL before 2pm ship the rate the same day." Only write that if the desk actually does it. A homepage promise that the inbox does not keep becomes the story at the dock.

Do not put a second button of equal weight beside it for "Track a shipment" or "Careers" or "Our technology." Tracking belongs in the header for people who already have a PRO number. The first screen belongs to the person who is deciding whether you get the freight.

## What the rest of the page is for

After the move and the quote, answer the three questions that decide a second look.

What do you haul, and what do you refuse? Equipment, regions, and the freight you will not take. Hazmat you are not set up for. Residential you will do only with a liftgate fee. International you do not touch. A refusal is more persuasive than a list of every mode you might someday offer.

How does a load actually run? Pickup window, linehaul cutoff, appointment versus first-come, where exceptions go. Three or four sentences in the dispatcher’s vocabulary. If you cannot write this without the words "end-to-end solutions," you are still writing for the team.

What does a problem look like when it is handled? One claim, one missed appointment, one reweigh. Who calls the operator, and how fast. This is the trust block. A certification logo does not replace it, though a certification you truly hold can sit beside the sentence as a fact.

Google's people-first guidance asks whether the page helps someone complete a task and whether it shows first-hand knowledge. A homepage that could be any carrier in any country fails the test. A homepage that names a cutoff and a refusal passes it, even if the photography is plain.

## Why the container photograph fails

A shipping container on water, or in a yard with no markings you could defend, is the default costume of this industry. It reassures a committee that the site "looks like logistics." The operator has seen that frame on every competitor, every software vendor, and every bank ad about trade finance. It does not answer whether you can make their Tuesday appointment.

The same is true of a handshake in a high-visibility vest, a tablet with an unreadable map, and a smiling driver who is not attached to a load. These pictures are warm and interchangeable. Interchangeable is the problem. The work is specific: a sealed trailer, a pallet count, a temperature logger, a residential street that needed a smaller truck.

If you do not yet have a photograph of your own work, use type. "Dry van, Midwest to the Southeast, appointment delivery, POD the same day." That sentence outperforms a rented container. You can commission the photograph when you have a load you are allowed to show. Do not rent the cliché while you wait.

When you do show equipment, show the equipment you run. A box truck if you are a box truck. A reefer unit if the product is cold. A flatbed with the kind of securement your operators will ask about. A picture of a mode you subcontract and never see is a claim you will be asked to repeat on the phone, under worse conditions.

## Speak to the person who books, not to a globe

The reader of the first screen is rarely "the supply chain." It is a coordinator, a plant scheduler, a warehouse lead, or an owner-operator looking for a partner on a lane. They use concrete nouns. Write those nouns.

Use their units. Pallets, pounds, cubic feet, miles, appointment windows. Do not open with a paragraph about disruption, resilience, or the future of freight. If a service is your actual edge, name it as a behavior: you answer after the cutoff, you do not reclass without a photo, you send the POD without a chase.

Regions beat "nationwide" when nationwide is a stretch. If you are strong in four states, the homepage should feel like those four states. An operator with freight in a fifth state can still ask. An operator in your lane should not have to guess whether you know the receiver's hours.

Internal names for products can stay inside the company. On the page, "priority" means a defined cutoff and a defined remedy when you miss it. If you cannot define both, you do not have a product. You have an adjective.

## A first screen you can hold against the draft

Read this shape against whatever the homepage says now.

One move, labeled with places and freight, marked as a sample if it must be. One sentence on what you refuse. One line on what a quote requires. A button that says request a quote. A response promise you have kept in the last month.

Everything else moves down or leaves. The award, the year founded, the software platform, the sustainability statement: each can earn a place later if it changes the operator's risk. None of them earn the first screen by default.

Then hand the phone to someone who has booked freight and does not work for you. Ask what you move and what they would tap. If they say "logistics" and cannot name a mode, the globe won. If they can name the mode and the button, the page is pointed the right way.

## Keep the homepage honest after the first campaign

The first version of this page often survives a week, until someone asks for a banner about a new terminal, a hiring push, or a software launch. Each banner is reasonable alone. Together they restore the globe problem: the first screen becomes a bulletin board, and the move drops below it.

Give the homepage a single owner who can say no. The test stays the same. Can an operator name the freight and the quote path without scrolling past news? If a banner fails that test, it can live on the page it belongs to, or in the note you send to people who already ship with you.

Review the sample move every quarter. A lane you no longer run, a mode you dropped, or a cutoff you changed should not remain as the proof. Stale proof is a kind of globe. It describes a company you used to be, in the spot where a live operator is making a decision.

The next page they open, if the move looks plausible, is the price. How to show the shape of that price, including what is not in it, is [a pricing page for a logistics company](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-logistics-company).

To see how a public site can lead with the work rather than a costume, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
